claims.text: A hybrid actively learned ML-potential and ab initio reweighting workflow can substantially reduce the cost of fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic calculations while retaining ab initio free-energy fidelity.
Active learning can identify strategically distinct configurations for static DFT evaluation and use them to retrain an interatomic potential.
The ML potential should be trained on ab initio configurations from both solid and liquid phases near the fusion point.
A DFT-trained interatomic potential can be used to run molecular-dynamics simulations.
Perturbative reweighting can restore ab initio-level phase free energies after sampling with an ML potential.
Near melting, the relevant solid and liquid free-energy landscapes contain significant vibrational-entropy, anharmonic, and electron–vibration-coupling contributions.
The proposed workflow is applicable from elemental and binary systems through high-entropy alloys containing up to five or six principal elements.
Training data spanning ordered solids and disordered liquids will capture all relevant entropy contributions and anharmonic effects.
Adding ab initio reweighting corrections to the ML potential landscape enforces the correct vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration-coupling physics.
The ML potential approximates the solid and liquid energy landscapes at a fraction of the cost of explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Reweighting corrects residual discrepancies between the ML potential and ab initio energetics.
The combined ML and reweighting strategy preserves free-energy contributions from vibrations and anharmonic motion.
Phase free energies and derived observables will agree with explicit ab initio molecular dynamics to within a few meV per atom.
The hybrid workflow will be three to ten times faster than explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The hybrid workflow will scale better to multicomponent systems than TOR-TILD.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations are computationally prohibitive, while TOR-TILD is slow for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The intended temperature domain is near and above fusion, where vibrational and anharmonic entropy contributions are critical.
Achievable fidelity depends on the quality and representativeness of the training set.
Systematic free-energy deviations greater than a few meV per atom, or melting-curve and latent-heat errors outside the anticipated bounds, would falsify the fidelity claim.
